```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE, fig.align = "center")
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
```

## Data

We use the `data.csv`: games between pairs of players, with columns `White`, `Black` and `Score` (1 = White win,
0.5 = draw, 0 = Black win).

```{r load-data}
games <- read.csv("data.csv")
str(games)

players   <- sort(unique(c(games$White, games$Black)))
n_players <- length(players)
idx       <- setNames(seq_along(players), players)

cat("Number of games  :", nrow(games), "\n")
cat("Number of players:", n_players, "\n")
```

---

## Challenge 1 — Does White have a first-mover advantage?

If there were no advantage to moving first, White's score in any game would average
0.5 (a win counts 1, a draw 0.5, a loss 0). We test `H0: E[Score] = 0.5` against the
two-sided alternative `H1` using the large-sample normal approximation (n is large enough
that the CLT (Central Limit Theorem) applies comfortably).

```{r challenge1}
white_mean <- mean(games$Score)
n          <- nrow(games)
se         <- sd(games$Score) / sqrt(n)
z_stat     <- (white_mean - 0.5) / se
p_value    <- 2 * (1 - pnorm(abs(z_stat)))

rates <- c(
  "White win" = mean(games$Score == 1),
  "Draw"      = mean(games$Score == 0.5),
  "Black win" = mean(games$Score == 0)
)

cat(sprintf("Mean White score     : %.4f  (0.5 = no advantage)\n", white_mean))
cat(sprintf("z = %.2f,  p-value = %.3g\n", z_stat, p_value))
```

**Conclusion.** White's average score (`r sprintf("%.4f", white_mean)`) is
significantly above 0.5 (z = `r sprintf("%.1f", z_stat)`, p < 0.001). The effect is
small in absolute size but, with `r format(n, big.mark=",")` games behind it, is
extremely unlikely to be chance. **White does have a first-mover advantage.**

---

## Challenge 2 — Point rating

A player's *point rating* is simply the total number of points earned: 1 per win,
0.5 per draw, 0 per loss, added up over every game the player took part in
(regardless of colour).

```{r challenge2-function}
point_rating <- function(games) {
  players <- sort(unique(c(games$White, games$Black)))
  idx     <- setNames(seq_along(players), players)
  pts     <- numeric(length(players))
  gp      <- numeric(length(players))

  wi <- idx[as.character(games$White)]
  bi <- idx[as.character(games$Black)]
  sc <- games$Score

  # vectorized accumulation (fast; no explicit per-row R loop)
  pts <- as.numeric(tapply(c(sc, 1 - sc), c(wi, bi), sum, default = 0))
  gp  <- as.numeric(table(factor(c(wi, bi), levels = seq_along(players))))

  data.frame(player = players, points = pts, games = gp)
}

pr <- point_rating(games)
summary(pr$points)
```

```{r challenge2-plot, fig.width=6, fig.height=4}
skewness <- function(x) mean((x - mean(x))^3) / sd(x)^3

ggplot(pr, aes(points)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 40, fill = "#4C78A8", color = "white") +
  labs(title = "Distribution of point ratings",
       subtitle = sprintf("skewness ≈ %.2f", skewness(pr$points)),
       x = "Point rating", y = "Number of players") +
  theme_minimal()
```

**Discussion.** The distribution is strongly **right-skewed**: most players have only
a handful of points, while a long tail of very active players has accumulated far
more. This is mechanical, not a sign of exceptional skill — a player who plays many
games will out-score a much stronger player who has only played a few, simply by
volume. Point rating conflates *activity* with *ability*, which motivates a rating
system that measures relative skill instead (Challenge 4).

---

## Challenge 3 — Proof that $\sum_i r_i = 0$ always

We are given, for every pair of players $(i,j)$ who face each other:

$$s_{i,j} + s_{j,i} = 1 \qquad \text{(actual scores of the two sides in one game sum to 1)}$$
$$\mu_{i,j} + \mu_{j,i} = 1 \qquad \text{(expected scores sum to 1, by construction of the logistic } \mu)$$

The Elo update after a single game between $i$ (as one side) and $j$ (as the other) is

$$r_i \leftarrow r_i + \kappa\,(s_{i,j} - \mu_{i,j}), \qquad r_j \leftarrow r_j + \kappa\,(s_{j,i} - \mu_{j,i}).$$

**Claim.** $\sum_k r_k$ is invariant (always equal to its initial value, which is 0
since every rating starts at 0).

**Proof.** Every update touches only the two ratings $r_i, r_j$ involved in that
game; every other player's rating is unchanged, so the only thing that can move the
total $\sum_k r_k$ is the sum of the two deltas applied in that game:

$$\Delta\!\left(\sum_k r_k\right) = \kappa(s_{i,j}-\mu_{i,j}) + \kappa(s_{j,i}-\mu_{j,i})
= \kappa\Big[(s_{i,j}+s_{j,i}) - (\mu_{i,j}+\mu_{j,i})\Big] = \kappa\,[\,1 - 1\,] = 0.$$

So a single game update leaves $\sum_k r_k$ exactly unchanged — the rating points
transferred to $i$ are precisely the rating points removed from $j$ (or vice versa):
Elo is a **closed, zero-sum** accounting system. Since $\sum_k r_k = 0$ at
initialization and every subsequent update (over every game, every epoch, in any
order) preserves the sum, by induction $\sum_k r_k = 0$ **at all times**. $\blacksquare$

---

## Challenge 4 — Elo rating

The proof above is exactly what lets the implementation be *optimized*: because
$\mu_{j,i}$ is always $1-\mu_{i,j}$ and the two deltas are always equal and opposite,
we only need to compute **one** expected score per game and apply it with a $\pm$
sign — there is never a need for a separate renormalization step to keep the ratings
zero-sum, because the update mechanics guarantee it automatically.

```{r challenge4-function}
elo_rating <- function(games, zeta = 400, kappa = 25, n_epochs = 10, seed = 1) {
  players <- sort(unique(c(games$White, games$Black)))
  idx     <- setNames(seq_along(players), players)
  wi <- idx[as.character(games$White)]
  bi <- idx[as.character(games$Black)]
  sc <- games$Score
  n_games <- length(sc)

  r <- numeric(length(players))   # all ratings start at 0 -> sum already 0
  set.seed(seed)

  for (epoch in seq_len(n_epochs)) {
    ord <- sample.int(n_games)          # re-shuffle game order each epoch
    for (g in ord) {
      i <- wi[g]; j <- bi[g]; s <- sc[g]
      mu    <- 1 / (1 + 10^(-(r[i] - r[j]) / zeta))  # only ONE expected score needed
      delta <- kappa * (s - mu)
      r[i]  <- r[i] + delta    # zero-sum: no separate mu_ji, no renormalization
      r[j]  <- r[j] - delta    #           ever needed -- see Challenge 3 proof
    }
  }
  data.frame(player = players, elo = r)
}

er <- elo_rating(games, n_epochs = 10)
summary(er$elo)
cat(sprintf("Sum of all Elo ratings (should be ~0): %.6g\n", sum(er$elo)))
```

```{r challenge4-plot, fig.width=6, fig.height=4}
ggplot(er, aes(elo)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 40, fill = "#F58518", color = "white") +
  labs(title = "Distribution of Elo ratings",
       subtitle = sprintf("skewness ≈ %.2f", skewness(er$elo)),
       x = "Elo rating", y = "Number of players") +
  theme_minimal()
```

**Why does the Elo distribution look so different from the point-rating
distribution?** Point rating only ever increases — it is a running total, bounded
below by 0 and unbounded above, so it is naturally right-skewed and driven mainly by
how many games a player has played (Challenge 2). Elo, by contrast, measures
*relative* skill: every update pushes a player's rating toward the level implied by
their actual results against the opposition they actually faced, and updates shrink
once a player's rating already matches their results. The zero-sum property forces
the whole population's ratings to balance around 0, producing a roughly
**symmetric, bell-shaped** spread of over- and under-performers, independent of how
many games any individual has played. And indeed `sum(er$elo)` comes out at machine
precision from zero, empirically confirming the Challenge 3 proof.

---

## Challenge 5 — Are point rating and Elo rating correlated? Do the same players top both lists?

```{r challenge5}
comb <- merge(pr, er, by = "player")

pearson_r  <- cor(comb$points, comb$elo, method = "pearson")
spearman_r <- cor(comb$points, comb$elo, method = "spearman")

cat(sprintf("Pearson correlation (points, elo)  = %.3f\n", pearson_r))
cat(sprintf("Spearman correlation (points, elo) = %.3f\n", spearman_r))
```

```{r challenge5-plot, fig.width=6, fig.height=4.5}
ggplot(comb, aes(points, elo)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.25, color = "#54A24B", size = 1) +
  labs(title = "Point rating vs Elo rating",
       subtitle = sprintf("Pearson r = %.2f, Spearman rho = %.2f", pearson_r, spearman_r),
       x = "Point rating", y = "Elo rating") +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r challenge5-top}
K <- 20
top_points <- comb$player[order(-comb$points)][1:K]
top_elo    <- comb$player[order(-comb$elo)][1:K]
overlap    <- intersect(top_points, top_elo)

knitr::kable(
  data.frame(
    Rank             = 1:K,
    `Top by points`  = top_points,
    `Top by Elo`     = top_elo,
    check.names = FALSE
  ),
  align = "rrr",
  caption = sprintf("Top-%d players by each rating (overlap: %d of %d players appear on both lists)",
                     K, length(overlap), K)
)
```

**Conclusion.** The two ratings are positively but only moderately correlated
(Pearson r ≈ `r sprintf("%.2f", pearson_r)`, Spearman rho ≈ `r sprintf("%.2f", spearman_r)`):
players who do well tend to score well under both systems, but the relationship is
far from 1-to-1, and the overlap between the two top-20 lists is partial, not
complete. This is consistent with Challenge 2's finding that point rating is
substantially inflated by games played: a very active, moderately-good player can
out-score (in points) a less active but genuinely stronger player, while Elo ranks
the latter higher.

---

## Challenge 6 — Does the number of games played affect rating?

```{r challenge6}
pearson_gp <- cor(comb$games, comb$points, method = "pearson")
pearson_ge <- cor(comb$games, comb$elo,    method = "pearson")
spear_gp   <- cor(comb$games, comb$points, method = "spearman")
spear_ge   <- cor(comb$games, comb$elo,    method = "spearman")

cat(sprintf("games vs points : Pearson r = %.3f, Spearman rho = %.3f\n", pearson_gp, spear_gp))
cat(sprintf("games vs elo    : Pearson r = %.3f, Spearman rho = %.3f\n", pearson_ge, spear_ge))
```

```{r challenge6-plots, fig.width=10, fig.height=4}
p1 <- ggplot(comb, aes(games, points)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.25, color = "#4C78A8", size = 1) +
  labs(title = sprintf("Games vs points (r=%.2f)", pearson_gp), x = "Games played", y = "Points") +
  theme_minimal()

p2 <- ggplot(comb, aes(games, elo)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.25, color = "#B279A2", size = 1) +
  labs(title = sprintf("Games vs Elo (r=%.2f)", pearson_ge), x = "Games played", y = "Elo") +
  theme_minimal()

gridExtra_available <- requireNamespace("gridExtra", quietly = TRUE)
if (gridExtra_available) {
  gridExtra::grid.arrange(p1, p2, ncol = 2)
} else {
  print(p1); print(p2)
}
```

```{r challenge6-quintiles}
comb$games_bucket <- cut(comb$games, breaks = quantile(comb$games, probs = seq(0, 1, 0.2)),
                          include.lowest = TRUE)

agg <- comb %>%
  group_by(games_bucket) %>%
  summarise(n = n(),
            mean_points = mean(points), sd_points = sd(points),
            mean_elo = mean(elo),       sd_elo = sd(elo))

knitr::kable(
  agg, digits = 2,
  col.names = c("Games played (range)", "Players (n)",
                "Avg. point rating", "Point rating SD",
                "Avg. Elo rating", "Elo rating SD"),
  align = "lrrrrr",
  caption = "Rating summary by games-played quintile"
)
```

**Conclusion.** The number of games played is, unsurprisingly, **very strongly**
related to point rating (r ≈ `r sprintf("%.2f", pearson_gp)`) — points are a running
total, so playing more games mechanically produces more points. Its relationship with
Elo is `r if (abs(pearson_ge) < 0.1) "weak" else "present but much smaller"`
(r ≈ `r sprintf("%.2f", pearson_ge)`): Elo is designed to be a measure of relative
skill rather than activity, so it is far less sensitive to how many games a player
has played. The games-played quintile table also shows that the *spread* (sd) of
Elo differs across quintiles — players with very few games have had fewer updates
to move their rating away from the initial value of 0, so their Elo is a noisier,
less settled estimate of their true skill than that of players with many games, even
though its central tendency is not strongly biased by activity the way points' is.

---

## Summary

| Challenge | Finding |
|---|---|
| 1 | White has a small but statistically significant scoring edge (mean score `r sprintf("%.3f", white_mean)` vs 0.5) |
| 2 | Point rating is right-skewed and driven heavily by number of games played |
| 3 | $\sum_i r_i = 0$ is an algebraic invariant of the Elo update rule (proved above) |
| 4 | Elo rating is symmetric/bell-shaped and empirically sums to ~0 |
| 5 | Points and Elo are only moderately correlated; their top-player lists only partly overlap |
| 6 | Games played strongly drives point rating but not the level of Elo — mainly its *precision* |
